stem: A 61-year-old man with long-standing gout has a week of right flank colic and visible hematuria. His urine pH is persistently 5.0. A plain abdominal film shows no stone, but CT shows a 6-mm stone in the right ureter. Urine sediment is examined under the microscope.
oneliner: 61M + gout + right flank colic + hematuria + urine pH 5.0 + stone invisible on plain film, seen on CT → ?
ask: Which crystal shape is most likely in the urine sediment?

options.E: Flat plates with a notched corner

whyNot.B: Hexagonal plates mean **cystine**, a faintly **radiopaque** stone from an amino acid transporter defect; his stone **did not show on plain film** and he has **gout**
whyNot.C: Coffin-lid prisms are **struvite**, which needs **alkaline** urine from a urea-splitting infection; his urine is **pH 5.0**
whyNot.D: Envelope shapes are **calcium oxalate**, a **radiopaque** stone; his stone **could not be seen on the plain film**
whyNot.E: Notched plates are **cholesterol**, seen with lipid-laden urine; this man has **colic from a stone**, with no heavy proteinuria described

why: Uric acid stones form in **acidic urine** and are **radiolucent**, so they vanish on plain film but show on CT. Gout raises the uric acid load, and the crystals are **rhomboid or rosette-shaped**.

idea.rule: Gout or high cell turnover, acidic urine and a radiolucent stone mean uric acid, with rhomboid crystals.
also: Uric acid stones are radiolucent, whereas calcium, struvite and cystine stones show on plain film
Tumor lysis and high cell turnover raise urinary uric acid
Potassium citrate raises urine pH and can dissolve uric acid stones
Low urine pH, not only high uric acid, drives crystal formation

stem: A 47-year-old woman has had urinary infections for 8 years and now has right flank pain. Urine pH is 7.6, and culture grows a urease-positive Proteus species. A plain film shows a large branching stone filling the renal pelvis and calyces. Urine sediment is examined under the microscope.
oneliner: 47F + 8 years of recurrent UTIs + flank pain + urine pH 7.6 + urease-positive Proteus + large branching radiopaque stone → ?
ask: Which crystal shape is most likely in the urine sediment?

options.E: Flat plates with a notched corner

whyNot.A: Hexagonal plates are **cystine**, from an amino acid transporter defect; she has a **urea-splitting infection and alkaline urine**
whyNot.B: Rhomboid crystals are **uric acid**, which forms only in **acidic** urine; hers is **pH 7.6**
whyNot.C: Envelope-shaped crystals are **calcium oxalate**, unrelated to infection; her stone is **branching with alkaline urine and Proteus**
whyNot.E: Notched plates are **cholesterol**, seen with lipid-laden nephrotic urine; her picture is an **infected branching stone with Proteus and pH 7.6**

why: **Proteus** splits urea with **urease**, releasing ammonia and making the urine **alkaline**. Magnesium ammonium phosphate (**struvite**) then precipitates as **coffin-lid** crystals and builds a branching **staghorn** stone.

idea.rule: Urease-positive infection makes alkaline urine, which gives struvite (coffin-lid) and a staghorn stone.
also: Other urease producers include Klebsiella, Staphylococcus saprophyticus and Ureaplasma
Treatment needs complete stone removal as well as antibiotics
Urine pH above 7 in an infected stone-former points to struvite

stem: A 7-year-old girl has passed her third kidney stone. Her urine is acidic and the cyanide-nitroprusside test is positive. Amino acid analysis of the urine shows high levels of ornithine, lysine and arginine. Urine sediment is examined under the microscope.
oneliner: 7F + third kidney stone + acidic urine + positive cyanide-nitroprusside + high urinary ornithine, lysine, arginine → ?
ask: Which crystal shape is most likely in the urine sediment?

options.D: Flat plates with a notched corner

whyNot.A: Rhomboid crystals are **uric acid**, linked to gout or high cell turnover; she has **excess dibasic amino acids and a positive nitroprusside test**
whyNot.B: Coffin-lid crystals are **struvite**, which needs **alkaline** urine and infection; her urine is **acidic**
whyNot.C: Envelope-shaped crystals are **calcium oxalate**; the **amino acid pattern and nitroprusside result** point elsewhere
whyNot.D: Notched plates are **cholesterol**, from lipid-rich urine; she has **recurrent stones with an amino aciduria**

why: Her **raised ornithine, lysine and arginine with cystine** (positive **nitroprusside**) and early recurrent stones mean **cystinuria**. Poorly soluble cystine crystallises as **flat hexagonal plates**.

idea.rule: Recurrent childhood stones with COLA amino aciduria are cystine, and the crystals are hexagonal.
also: Cystinuria is autosomal recessive, with a defect in the proximal tubule transporter for cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine
Treatment is high fluid intake, urine alkalinisation and tiopronin
Hexagonal urine crystals are essentially specific to cystine

stem: A 44-year-old man has a headache and blurred vision. His blood pressure is 220/130 mm Hg, with papilledema on eye examination. Creatinine has climbed from 1.4 to 6.0 mg/dL over two weeks, and urine shows mild proteinuria. He has had no recent vascular procedures. He dies of a stroke, and at autopsy the kidney surface is dotted with tiny hemorrhages. Kidney histology is examined.
oneliner: 44M + BP 220/130 + papilledema + creatinine 1.4 to 6.0 in 2 weeks + mild proteinuria + petechiae on kidney surface → ?
ask: Which vessel finding on kidney histology is most likely?

options.B: Onion-skin smooth muscle layering of arterioles
options.C: Calcification of the media of medium-sized arteries
options.D: String-of-beads narrowing of the main renal artery

whyNot.A: Hyaline change is the lesion of **slow, long-standing** hypertension; he has a **creatinine rising over two weeks** with petechiae
whyNot.C: Medial calcification **does not narrow the lumen**, so it cannot explain a creatinine that rose within **two weeks**
whyNot.D: String-of-beads is **fibromuscular dysplasia** of the main renal artery, usually in **young women**; his clue is **extreme pressure with papilledema** and a petechial kidney surface
whyNot.E: Cholesterol emboli follow **vascular procedures or anticoagulation**; he **had none**, and his pressure is the clue

answer: Onion-skin smooth muscle layering of arterioles (hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis)
why: Severe, abrupt hypertension with organ injury (**malignant hypertension**) causes **hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis**, an **onion-skin** layering of smooth muscle, sometimes with **fibrinoid necrosis**. The kidney fails quickly and shows a **flea-bitten** surface.

idea.rule: Slow benign hypertension gives hyaline arteriolosclerosis; rapid malignant hypertension gives hyperplastic (onion-skin) arteriolosclerosis.
also: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis also occurs in diabetes
Chronic benign hypertension gives small, finely granular kidneys
Malignant hypertension can bring microangiopathic hemolysis with schistocytes
Malignant hypertension is a blood pressure over about 180/120 with acute organ damage
